screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how to make a Java program choose actions and repeat work. Control flow lets a program behave like a recipe: some steps run once, some run only when a condition is true, and others repeat until a condition changes. We will study conditional statements that route execution, the switch statement that offers multi-way branching and its common fall-through pitfall, and three loop forms: for, while, and do-while. You will also learn how break and continue change the normal loop flow and how to spot and fix infinite loops. Expect concrete examples: checking a temperature, iterating a list of fruits, and building a simple menu-driven application that uses a loop and switch together. Understanding these constructs is essential because they make programs interactive and efficient, and they prevent runtime problems like unending loops or incorrect branching. Listen for one common misconception: missing break in switch or forgetting to update a loop variable. As you move through the lesson, think about how each construct maps to everyday instructions and where misuse can hide bugs.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will implement conditional logic and structured branching, and you'll know when to choose a switch over a long if-else chain. You will practice writing if, else if, and else statements that evaluate boolean expressions, and you will handle multiple cases with switch while avoiding the common fall-through mistake. You will also write for loops for counted iteration and enhanced for loops to walk collections, with attention to off-by-one errors. Each objective links to a practical example so you can see these constructs in action. For instance, use if-else to compare temperatures and switch to handle menu choices. A key misconception to avoid is assuming switch always isolates cases; without break, execution falls through. Another is believing a loop always runs at least once: only do-while guarantees that. These objectives will help you read and write safer, clearer Java code and spot control flow bugs in testing and debugging.

screens.title: If / Else: Conditional Branching
screens.narratorSegment: An if-else statement evaluates a boolean expression and executes one block when the condition is true and another when it is false. This is the most direct way to make choices in Java. Conceptually, read an if condition as a question: if the question is true, do the first block; otherwise evaluate the next question or run the else block. A concrete example is comparing a temperature variable: if the temperature is above a threshold then print a warm message, else if it's above a lower threshold print a pleasant message, else print chilly. A common misconception is that an else-if chain will test all conditions even after one succeeds; in reality, once a true condition runs, the rest of the chain is skipped. Another mistake is omitting braces for multi-line blocks; if you later add a second statement without braces the logic can silently change. Practice by writing a small nested if to validate input, but avoid deep nesting — break logic into helper methods instead. Key takeaway: use if-else for clear boolean decisions, prefer braces for all blocks, and test boundary conditions to avoid off-by-one or mis-evaluated ranges.

keyIdea.title: If-else rule
keyIdea.text: If-else evaluates conditions in order; the first true branch runs and the rest are skipped—always use braces to avoid hidden errors.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › If / Else
Definition and structure
An if statement runs a block when a boolean expression is true. Else-if and else form a chain evaluated in order.
Example
int temperature = 25;
if (temperature > 30) {
  System.out.println("It's a hot day!");
} else if (temperature > 20) {
  System.out.println("It's a pleasant day.");
} else {
  System.out.println("It's a bit chilly.");
}
Explanation
  • Conditions are boolean expressions that evaluate to true or false.
  • Once a true branch runs, subsequent else-if blocks are ignored.
  • Always use braces to protect against future edits that add lines.
Common mistake
Omitting braces for a multi-statement block and later adding statements without updating braces causes silent logic errors.
Key Takeaway
Use if-else for direct branching. Favor clarity: short conditions, descriptive variable names, and braces on every block.

screens.title: Switch and Fall-Through
screens.narratorSegment: A switch statement offers a clearer structure when a single variable can take many discrete values. It compares the switch expression to case labels and executes the matching case. The crucial behavior to learn is fall-through: without a break, execution continues into the next case and executes its statements too. That makes switch concise when cases intentionally share code, but also makes it a frequent source of bugs when break is forgotten. For example, when mapping a grade character to feedback, group similar grades together and use break after the shared block. Another common misconception is that default runs only when no case matches; that's true, but if you fall through from an earlier case you may still reach default. Also remember which types are allowed for the switch expression: primitive integrals, char, String, and enums. To avoid bugs, place break at the end of each case unless you intentionally want fall-through and comment it clearly. Key takeaway: use switch for value-based branching, explicitly control fall-through with break, and add a default case to handle unexpected values. Switch and Fall-Through means switch matches a single expression against constant case labels; always consider break to avoid unintended fall-through.. In practical terms, multi-way branching and why break matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Switch
Switch structure
Use switch for a variable with many possible constant values. Control fall-through explicitly.
char grade = 'B';
switch (grade) {
  case 'A':
    System.out.println("Excellent!");
    break;
  case 'B':
  case 'C':
    System.out.println("Well done.");
    break;
  default:
    System.out.println("Invalid grade.");
}
Explanation
  • Each case is a constant label; the expression type must be compatible.
  • break exits the switch; without it, code runs into the next case.
  • default handles unmatched values and helps avoid unexpected behavior.
Common mistake
Forgetting break causes fall-through, which can unexpectedly execute later assignments or prints.
Key Takeaway
Use switch when branching on a single value; place break deliberately and include default to catch unknowns.

screens.title: For Loops: Counting and Collections
screens.narratorSegment: A for loop provides a compact way to iterate when you know how many times to run or when you need an index. It has three parts: initialization executed once, a condition checked before each iteration, and an update run after each iteration. For example, printing numbers from one to five uses initialization at one, condition i less than or equal to five, and an increment. A frequent error is off-by-one: choose < or <= carefully depending on start and end values. When iterating arrays or collections, consider the enhanced for loop which hides the index and reads more clearly. The enhanced loop is ideal for read-only processing, but if you need the index or to modify elements by position, use the indexed for loop. A misconception is to assume enhanced for always faster; its benefit is readability and fewer mistakes, not performance guarantees. Practice both forms: indexed for precise control and enhanced for simple element processing. Key takeaway: match the loop form to the task — indexed loops for positions, enhanced for for straightforward element traversal. For Loops: Counting and Collections means initialization, condition, and update control a counted loop. use enhanced for for simple collection traversal when index access is unnecessary.. In practical terms, initialization, condition, update — and the enhanced for loop. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: For loop pattern
keyIdea.text: Initialization, condition, and update control a counted loop. Use enhanced for for simple collection traversal when index access is unnecessary.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › For Loops
Counting loop example
// Print numbers from 1 to 5
for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  System.out.println("Count: " + i);
}

// Iterate array with index
String[] fruits = {"Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"};
for (int i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) {
  System.out.println("Fruit: " + fruits[i]);
}

// Enhanced for loop
for (String fruit : fruits) {
  System.out.println("Fruit (for-each): " + fruit);
}
Key points
  • Initialization runs once; condition is checked before each iteration.
  • Use < or <= deliberately to avoid off-by-one bugs.
  • Enhanced for simplifies iteration when index is not needed.
Common mistake
Using the wrong comparison can skip the final element or cause off-by-one errors.
Key Takeaway
Choose an indexed for loop when you need positions; use the enhanced for for cleaner element access.

screens.title: While and Do-While Loops
screens.narratorSegment: While and do-while loops are condition-controlled repetition constructs. A while loop checks the condition before each iteration, so if the condition starts false the body never runs. This is useful when you only want to execute while a condition holds — for example, reading input until it becomes valid. The do-while loop checks after the body, guaranteeing at least one execution. Use this when you need an initial action like prompting a user and then repeating based on their response. A critical risk with both is failing to update the condition variable inside the body, which creates an infinite loop. For while, ensure state changes or break conditions occur; for do-while, remember the first run always happens so validate initial values if necessary. A common learner error is assuming while and do-while behave the same; test both with an initially false condition to see the difference. Key takeaway: pick while when entry is conditional, and do-while when you must perform at least one iteration. While and Do-While Loops means while checks before running; do-while checks after. use do-while when you require one guaranteed execution.. In practical terms, condition-first vs condition-after iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: While checks before running; do-while checks after. Use do-while when you require one guaranteed execution.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › While / Do-While
While loop
int count = 0;
while (count < 5) {
  System.out.println("While count: " + count);
  count++; // update the condition variable
}
If the initial condition is false, the body never runs. Ensure the condition changes inside the loop to avoid infinite loops.
Do-while loop
int i = 0;
do {
  System.out.println("Do-While i: " + i);
  i++;
} while (i < 0); // runs once even though condition is false
Use when the block must execute at least once, such as prompting a user then validating the input after the first read.
Common mistake
Forgetting to update the loop variable inside a while loop produces an infinite loop. Always verify termination conditions during testing.

screens.title: Break vs Continue
screens.narratorSegment: Break and continue change the normal loop flow in different ways. Break exits the innermost loop or switch immediately, transferring control to the statement after the loop. Continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next iteration, running the loop's update step before re-evaluating the condition. A concrete example: in a for loop counting zero to nine, using continue when the index equals two will skip printing two but continue with three, while break at two stops the loop entirely. Misunderstandings often arise when learners overuse these statements to patch logic; they can make reasoning harder if scattered across nested loops. Prefer clear conditions and early returns from methods for readability where possible. Another subtlety: break also exits switch, which is why missing break in switch can cause fall-through. Key takeaway: use continue to skip an iteration and break to stop the loop; document intent when used inside complex loops. Break vs Continue means continue skips to the next iteration; break exits the loop. use them for clear, localized control changes, not global flow fixes.. In practical terms, how they change loop execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Continue skips to the next iteration; break exits the loop. Use them for clear, localized control changes, not global flow fixes.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Break / Continue
Example: continue
for (int k = 0; k < 5; k++) {
  if (k == 2) {
    continue; // skip printing for k=2
  }
  System.out.println("K: " + k);
}
Example: break
for (int j = 0; j < 10; j++) {
  if (j == 5) {
    break; // exit loop when j is 5
  }
  System.out.println("J: " + j);
}
Key Takeaway
Use continue to skip an iteration, break to stop the loop. Keep usage localized and documented to maintain clarity in loops.

screens.title: Common Mistakes: Off-by-One, Missing Braces, and Fall-Through
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow mistakes are common but easy to catch with careful checks. Off-by-one errors happen when loop boundaries are incorrect: using less-than instead of less-than-or-equal can omit the final element. Fixes often involve checking array length, start index, and whether the loop should include the boundary. Missing braces is another classic: a single-line if without braces may work initially but when a second statement is added it will not be part of the intended block, producing subtle bugs. Always use braces for maintainability. Fall-through in switch occurs when break is omitted; this can silently change variable values or outputs. If you intentionally rely on fall-through, annotate it with a comment so reviewers know it is deliberate. To debug, add small print statements or run step-by-step in a debugger to inspect the condition variable and loop progress. Key takeaway: write clear boundaries, always use braces, and document intentional fall-through to reduce surprises for future readers. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Common Mistakes
Off-by-one
Check whether loops should use < or <= and whether indices start at zero or one. Confirm with small inputs.
Missing braces
Always add braces even for single-line blocks to avoid logic changes when modifying code later.
Fall-through in switch
If break is missing, subsequent cases run too. Ensure break is present or comment intentional fall-through clearly for reviewers.
Key Takeaway
Write defensively: test edges, prefer braces, and document exceptions to normal control flow so bugs are visible during review.

screens.title: Loop Anatomy and Off-by-One Examples
screens.narratorSegment: Every for loop follows the same anatomy: initialize the index, check the condition, run the body, then perform the update. Knowing this sequence helps you reason about off-by-one or skipped iterations. For example, iterating an array of length n usually starts at zero and runs while the index is less than n — that visits all valid indices. If you mistakenly use less than or equal to n, you'll read out of bounds. Another example is counting from one to five: start at one and use less than or equal to five. A practical way to test correctness is to run the loop with small sizes and print the index to confirm the exact values produced. Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › MenuApp Starter
Starter code template
This template shows a complete menu loop that uses switch and for/if logic for actions.
import java.util.Scanner; // Don't forget this import!

public class MenuApp {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
        boolean running = true;

        while (running) {
            System.out.println("
--- Menu ---");
            System.out.println("1. Check Even/Odd");
            System.out.println("2. Calculate Factorial");
            System.out.println("3. Exit");
            System.out.print("Enter your choice: ");

            int choice = scanner.nextInt(); // Read user's choice

            switch (choice) {
                case 1:
                    System.out.print("Enter an integer to check (Even/Odd): ");
                    int num = scanner.nextInt();
                    if (num % 2 == 0) {
                        System.out.println(num + " is Even.");
                    } else {
                        System.out.println(num + " is Odd.");
                    }
                    break;
                case 2:
                    System.out.print("Enter a non-negative integer for factorial: ");
                    int factorialNum = scanner.nextInt();
                    if (factorialNum < 0) {
                        System.out.println("Factorial is not defined for negative numbers.");
                    } else {
                        long factorialResult = 1; // Use long for potentially large factorials
                        for (int i = 1; i <= factorialNum; i++) {
                            factorialResult *= i;
                        }
                        System.out.println("Factorial of " + factorialNum + " is: " + factorialResult);
                    }
                    break;
                case 3:
                    System.out.println("Exiting application. Goodbye!");
                    running = false; // Set running to false to exit the while loop
                    break;
                default:
                    System.out.println("Invalid choice. Please try again.");
            }
        }
        scanner.close(); // Close the scanner to release resources
    }
}

screens.title: Infinite Loops: Detection and Fixes
screens.narratorSegment: An infinite loop occurs when a loop's termination condition never becomes false, causing the program to repeat forever. This often happens when the loop variable is never updated or when the condition is constructed incorrectly. For example, forgetting to increment a counter or using the wrong comparison operator produces a loop that never ends. To detect infinite loops, run with small inputs, add logging of the loop variable, or step through with a debugger to see if state changes as expected. Fixes include ensuring updates occur inside the loop, using break with a clear guard for emergency exit, or refactoring the loop into a for loop with a well-defined index. Be cautious with break as a patch; prefer correcting the underlying condition. Also consider adding sanity checks such as a maximum iteration count for defensive programming. Key takeaway: design loops with clear termination conditions, test boundary behavior, and use logging or debuggers to inspect variables if the loop seems to never finish. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how to make a Java program choose actions and repeat work. Control flow lets a program behave like a recipe: some steps run once, some run only when a condition is true, and others repeat until a condition changes. We will study conditional statements that route execution, the switch statement that offers multi-way branching and its common fall-through pitfall, and three loop forms: for, while, and do-while. You will also learn how break and continue change the normal loop flow and how to spot and fix infinite loops. Expect concrete examples: checking a temperature, iterating a list of fruits, and building a simple menu-driven application that uses a loop and switch together. Understanding these constructs is essential because they make programs interactive and efficient, and they prevent runtime problems like unending loops or incorrect branching. Listen for one common misconception: missing break in switch or forgetting to update a loop variable. As you move through the lesson, think about how each construct maps to everyday instructions and where misuse can hide bugs.

By the end of this chapter you will implement conditional logic and structured branching, and you'll know when to choose a switch over a long if-else chain. You will practice writing if, else if, and else statements that evaluate boolean expressions, and you will handle multiple cases with switch while avoiding the common fall-through mistake. You will also write for loops for counted iteration and enhanced for loops to walk collections, with attention to off-by-one errors. Each objective links to a practical example so you can see these constructs in action. For instance, use if-else to compare temperatures and switch to handle menu choices. A key misconception to avoid is assuming switch always isolates cases; without break, execution falls through. Another is believing a loop always runs at least once: only do-while guarantees that. These objectives will help you read and write safer, clearer Java code and spot control flow bugs in testing and debugging.

These next objectives focus on practical loop control and safety. You will construct for loops for counted repetition and enhanced for loops for collections, and you will use while and do-while when conditions determine repetition. Practice updating loop variables and writing correct loop conditions to avoid off-by-one errors and infinite loops. You will also learn to use break to exit early from loops or switch blocks and continue to skip the remainder of the current iteration. A common trap is overusing break or continue, which can obscure the logic; instead, prefer clear loop conditions and small helper methods when possible. Finally, you'll apply these skills in a hands-on menu activity that reads user input and dispatches actions. These objectives are designed to make your code predictable, testable, and easier to debug when unexpected input arrives.

An if-else statement evaluates a boolean expression and executes one block when the condition is true and another when it is false. This is the most direct way to make choices in Java. Conceptually, read an if condition as a question: if the question is true, do the first block; otherwise evaluate the next question or run the else block. A concrete example is comparing a temperature variable: if the temperature is above a threshold then print a warm message, else if it's above a lower threshold print a pleasant message, else print chilly. A common misconception is that an else-if chain will test all conditions even after one succeeds; in reality, once a true condition runs, the rest of the chain is skipped. Another mistake is omitting braces for multi-line blocks; if you later add a second statement without braces the logic can silently change. Practice by writing a small nested if to validate input, but avoid deep nesting — break logic into helper methods instead. Key takeaway: use if-else for clear boolean decisions, prefer braces for all blocks, and test boundary conditions to avoid off-by-one or mis-evaluated ranges.

A switch statement offers a clearer structure when a single variable can take many discrete values. It compares the switch expression to case labels and executes the matching case. The crucial behavior to learn is fall-through: without a break, execution continues into the next case and executes its statements too. That makes switch concise when cases intentionally share code, but also makes it a frequent source of bugs when break is forgotten. For example, when mapping a grade character to feedback, group similar grades together and use break after the shared block. Another common misconception is that default runs only when no case matches; that's true, but if you fall through from an earlier case you may still reach default. Also remember which types are allowed for the switch expression: primitive integrals, char, String, and enums. To avoid bugs, place break at the end of each case unless you intentionally want fall-through and comment it clearly. Key takeaway: use switch for value-based branching, explicitly control fall-through with break, and add a default case to handle unexpected values. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A for loop provides a compact way to iterate when you know how many times to run or when you need an index. It has three parts: initialization executed once, a condition checked before each iteration, and an update run after each iteration. For example, printing numbers from one to five uses initialization at one, condition i less than or equal to five, and an increment. A frequent error is off-by-one: choose < or <= carefully depending on start and end values. When iterating arrays or collections, consider the enhanced for loop which hides the index and reads more clearly. The enhanced loop is ideal for read-only processing, but if you need the index or to modify elements by position, use the indexed for loop. Use this when you need an initial action like prompting a user and then repeating based on their response. An infinite loop occurs when a loop's termination condition never becomes false, causing the program to repeat forever. This often happens when the loop variable is never updated or when the condition is constructed incorrectly. For example, forgetting to increment a counter or using the wrong comparison operator produces a loop that never ends. To detect infinite loops, run with small inputs, add logging of the loop variable, or step through with a debugger to see if state changes as expected. Fixes include ensuring updates occur inside the loop, using break with a clear guard for emergency exit, or refactoring the loop into a for loop with a well-defined index. Be cautious with break as a patch; prefer correcting the underlying condition. Also consider adding sanity checks such as a maximum iteration count for defensive programming. Key takeaway: design loops with clear termination conditions, test boundary behavior, and use logging or debuggers to inspect variables if the loop seems to never finish. Always use braces for if, else, and loop blocks, even when they contain a single statement; this avoids mistakes during later edits. Here are the essential concepts to remember. First, conditional statements let programs choose between actions based on boolean conditions. Use if-else for chains of tests and switch for value-based multi-way branching, always guarding against fall-through. Second, loops automate repetition: for loops are best when the number of iterations is known, while and do-while loops are condition-driven; do-while guarantees one execution. Third, break and continue let you alter loop execution: break exits early and continue skips to the next iteration. Use them sparingly and document intent. Finally, test boundary cases and use braces and small methods to keep control flow readable. These practices prevent common bugs like off-by-one errors, missing braces, fall-through, and infinite loops. Hold these ideas as you write and review code — they will make programs safer and simpler to reason about.

A final set of reminders will help you code confidently. Always include a default branch in switch to guard against unexpected values. When looping, test with small inputs and edge cases like empty arrays or minimal bounds to confirm behavior. Use the enhanced for loop for cleaner traversal when indices are unnecessary, and use indexed loops if you need to access or modify elements by position. When you write interactive loops, close resources such as scanners after the loop ends to avoid leaks. If you detect an infinite loop during testing, add logging to inspect the loop variable or a maximum iteration guard to stop runaway behavior. Lastly, prefer clarity: a few extra lines that document intent or use braces are worth avoiding future bugs. Carry these checks into your workflow to prevent common control flow problems.
